lesson.title: Bar Graphs: Picturing Categories Side by Side
lesson.summary: A bar graph displays the distribution of a categorical variable as separated bars whose heights represent frequency or relative frequency, making the most and least common categories easy to spot.
lesson.body:
A bar graph is the standard picture of the distribution of a categorical variable. Each category gets its own bar, and the height of the bar represents either the frequency or the relative frequency of that category. Because the categories of a categorical variable, such as eye color or favorite subject, have no natural numeric order or continuous scale between them, the bars in a bar graph are drawn with visible gaps between them, signaling that the categories are separate and distinct rather than points along a continuous number line.

Building a bar graph starts exactly where a frequency table leaves off. Once you know the frequency or relative frequency for each category, you draw a horizontal axis listing the categories and a vertical axis showing the count or proportion scale, then draw one bar per category reaching up to its corresponding value. Because there is no required order to the categories on the horizontal axis, bars are often rearranged from tallest to shortest to make the graph easier to read at a glance, something that would not make sense for quantitative data with a fixed numeric order.

Using the eye color distribution from earlier, 20 students with brown 9, blue 6, green 3, and hazel 2, a bar graph would show four separated bars: a tall one reaching to 9 above Brown, a slightly shorter one reaching to 6 above Blue, a short one reaching to 3 above Green, and the shortest reaching to 2 above Hazel. Reading the graph, brown is instantly visible as the most common eye color in this group, and hazel as the least common, without needing to compare raw numbers in a table.

A common mistake is confusing a bar graph with a histogram, which is covered later in this course. A bar graph displays a categorical variable with gaps between bars and categories that can be reordered freely, while a histogram displays a quantitative variable grouped into numeric intervals, with bars that touch because the underlying scale is continuous. Mixing up these two graphs, or removing the gaps from a bar graph, blurs an important distinction: categorical data has no meaningful in between the categories, while quantitative data does.

Bar graphs are especially useful for comparing categories directly, and a double or side by side bar graph can extend the idea to compare the same categorical variable across two different groups, such as eye color distributions for two different classes, by placing paired bars next to each other for each category. This graphing tool, built directly from the frequency table and relative frequency concepts, remains one of the most common ways categorical data is communicated in news articles, research reports, and everyday charts.

A bar graph can also be drawn using relative frequencies instead of raw frequencies on the vertical axis, which produces bars with exactly the same relative heights and overall shape, just rescaled onto a 0 to 1 or 0 to 100 percent axis. This relative frequency version is especially useful when comparing two bar graphs built from groups of very different sizes, since it removes the size of each group from the comparison entirely, the same benefit relative frequency provided earlier when comparing frequency tables directly.
